---
title: "Habit"
---

External habit makes risk aversion move with the surplus of consumption
over a slow-moving habit stock. In good times surplus is high and
investors are willing to hold risk. In bad times surplus is low,
marginal utility is high, and they demand a large premium. Campbell and
Cochrane (1999) use that mechanism to match the postwar equity premium
at $\gamma = 2$, which power utility cannot.

The claim to aggregate consumption is equity. The one-period claim is
the bill. Consumption growth is i.i.d. The only state is log surplus
$s_t$. Returns never enter the calibration.

```{python}
import geap

model = geap.CampbellCochraneModel()
res = model.solve()
print(res.compare("equity", "bill").summary())
```

Power utility on a two-state chain, at the same $\gamma = 2$, produces
a premium well below one point. Habit produces several points and keeps
the bill near 0.94 percent a year (Campbell and Cochrane 1999).
Long-run risks gets a large premium from persistent consumption news
instead of from a time-varying surplus.

## Surplus and sensitivity

$$
S_t = \frac{C_t - X_t}{C_t}, \qquad
s_{t+1} = (1-\phi)\bar s + \phi s_t + \lambda(s_t)\,(\Delta c_{t+1}-g).
$$

$\lambda(s)$ is chosen so the bill is locally constant ($b = 0$ in
their notation). Steady-state surplus is
$\bar S = \sigma\sqrt{\gamma/(1-\phi)}$.

## Limits

- Habit is external: the household does not internalise the effect of
  consumption on $X$.
- The default prices only the consumption claim and the bill. A
  cross-section of dividend claims is not in this family yet.
- Unconditional moments come from a simulated monthly path after the
  price-consumption function is solved on a surplus grid. They move
  slightly with the grid and the draw.

Source: Campbell and Cochrane (1999).
